client: I've been having a really hard time since my grandmother passed away a few weeks ago. I keep losing focus at work — like, I'll be in the middle of something and just completely blank out, and then I feel this wave of sadness that's hard to push through. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I should at least try.
therapist: It takes real courage to show up and try, even when part of you isn't sure it will help — and I'm really glad you did. Grief has a way of quietly pulling us out of the present moment, and those waves of sadness you're describing at work make complete sense given what you've been carrying. I'd love to understand a little more about what's been going on — when one of those moments hits and you blank out, what kinds of thoughts tend to surface for you, if any?

client: Honestly, when those moments hit, it's usually something small that sets it off — like someone mentions their weekend plans with their family, or I hear a song that my mom used to hum. And then my mind just goes somewhere else entirely, like I'm half-present in the room but mostly just... back there, wishing I'd said more before she passed. There's this guilt that kind of wraps around everything, like I should have visited more, called more, been more — and I can't seem to shake it no matter how much I try to logic my way out of it.
therapist: That guilt you're describing — the "I should have done more" — is one of the most painful and common parts of grief, and it sounds like it's become a kind of weight you're carrying constantly. It's really telling that even when you *try* to logic your way out of it, it doesn't budge — that's because grief isn't just a thinking problem, it's deeply felt, and the guilt often holds a kind of love inside it too. I'm curious — when you imagine what your grandmother would say if she could hear those thoughts you're having about yourself, what do you think she'd tell you?

client: I've thought about that before, actually — what she would say. And I know, logically, she'd probably tell me I was a good granddaughter and that she loved me. But it's like... I can hear the words in my head and they just don't land, they don't actually make me feel any better, which almost makes me feel worse because then I think, why can't I just believe it?
therapist: That frustration of *knowing* something but not being able to *feel* it is such a real and painful gap — and the fact that it's not working doesn't mean anything is wrong with you, it actually means the grief is still very fresh and very deep. In CBT we sometimes call this the head-heart lag, where our rational mind gets there first but our emotional self needs more time and a different kind of processing to catch up. I'm wondering — do you think part of you feels like believing her words would mean letting go of the guilt, and maybe that guilt is somehow keeping you connected to her?

client: That question kind of stopped me in my tracks, honestly. Because yeah, I think you might be right — like if I let go of the guilt, it almost feels like I'm admitting that what happened is just... done, and she's really gone, and I have to move on without her. The guilt is awful but it's also the last thing tying me to her, and I don't know how to grieve without it.
therapist: What you just named is so profound and so human — the guilt isn't just guilt, it's become a way of staying close to her, and of course letting it go feels terrifying when it's been holding that connection. But I want to gently offer this: what if the love you have for her doesn't have to leave when the guilt does — what if grief can actually be carried *through* love rather than through pain? What do you think it might look like to stay connected to your grandmother in a way that honors her, without it having to hurt you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me really wants to believe that's possible. But honestly, it feels almost... disloyal, like if I stop hurting over how things ended with her, it means I didn't care enough or that I'm just moving on and forgetting her. I don't even know what carrying love without pain would look like for me — it's been so long since the two felt separate.
therapist: The idea that stopping the pain means you didn't care enough is such a tender and understandable fear, but I want to gently challenge it — your love for her was built over a lifetime of moments, not measured by how much you suffer after she's gone. Many people find that as the pain softens, what's left isn't emptiness or forgetting, but something quieter and more sustaining — like carrying a person with you rather than mourning them. I'm curious, when you think about the relationship you had with her *before* the loss and guilt took over, what's one memory or quality of hers that you'd want to keep close to you?

client: I have to sit with that for a second, because part of me really wants to push back and say that the suffering is the proof of love... but I hear what you're saying, and it does something to me. When I think about her before all of this, before the hospital visits and the guilt about not calling more often, I keep coming back to the way she laughed at her own jokes before she even finished telling them. She'd just lose it, completely, and it was impossible not to laugh with her, even when the joke was terrible. I guess that's the version of her I'm terrified of losing if I stop holding onto the pain so tightly.
therapist: That image of her laughing at her own jokes before she even finished them — that's *her*, and it's so alive in the way you just described it that I can almost feel her presence in the room. I want to reflect something back to you: you just kept her with you completely, not through pain, but through joy and specificity and love — and that memory didn't need the guilt to exist. What if that laugh, and all the moments like it, are actually *safer* from being lost than you think — because they're already so vividly part of you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and for a second there, when I was describing her laugh, it did feel like she was almost here again, which was... I don't know, both beautiful and kind of devastating at the same time. But I'm scared that if I stop holding onto the guilt, it's like I'm admitting I've moved on, or that losing her is somehow okay, and it's not okay. I guess I just don't fully trust that the good memories are enough to keep her close without the pain anchoring everything.
therapist: That moment when she felt almost present again through her laugh — that's not nothing, that's actually something really important your heart is showing you. And I want to honor what you said: losing her is *not* okay, and nothing about healing asks you to pretend it is — grieving fully and loving her fully can both be true at the same time, without one canceling the other. I'm wondering, when you imagine a version of yourself a year from now who still misses her deeply but has made a little more room for that laugh alongside the pain, what does that person look like to you?

client: I sit with that question for a second because honestly my first instinct is to push it away. Like, imagining a "better" version of myself feels almost like a betrayal, as if I'm already planning to leave her behind. But I guess... that person probably still talks about her, still keeps her photo up, still gets hit by those random waves of missing her — they just don't feel guilty every time something makes them smile.
therapist: What you just described — still talking about her, keeping her photo up, letting the waves come, but not punishing yourself for smiling — that's not leaving her behind, that's actually a beautiful and sustainable way of loving someone who isn't here anymore. And I notice you found that image yourself, even through the resistance, which tells me some part of you already knows that version of you is possible. What would it mean to treat that vision not as a betrayal, but as something your grandmother — the one who laughed at her own jokes — might have actually wanted for you?

client: I mean... when you put it that way, I can almost hear her laughing at me for being so dramatic about it. She was always the one telling me not to take everything so seriously, so yeah, maybe she would have wanted me to smile at something stupid on TV without feeling like I was erasing her. But it still feels like a leap, you know? Like intellectually I can follow the logic, but in the moment when the guilt hits, it doesn't feel like logic, it just feels like I'm doing something wrong.
therapist: She sounds like she was wonderful — and the fact that you can almost hear her teasing you gently is her still being *with* you, right now, in this conversation. You've named something really important though: the gap between understanding something and feeling it in those raw moments is exactly where the real work happens, and that's not a flaw in you, it's just how deeply this is held. I'm wondering if it might help to have something small and concrete ready for those moments when the guilt hits — almost like a little anchor back to her laugh rather than her loss — what do you think might work as that kind of reminder for you?

client: I like the idea of an anchor, but I'm not sure what that would even look like for me in practice. Like, when the guilt hits, it hits fast and hard, and I can't really imagine myself stopping to look at a photo or something and suddenly feeling better. It almost feels too simple for something this heavy.
therapist: You're right that it needs to be something real, not a quick fix that feels hollow against something this heavy — and I appreciate you pushing back on that, because it means we find something that actually fits *you*. The anchor doesn't have to be soft or sweet; for some people it's a phrase, even something she might have said, or just a single breath where you let yourself acknowledge both things at once — "I miss her *and* she'd want me to be okay." What if the anchor wasn't about feeling better immediately, but just about creating one small moment of pause before the guilt fully takes over — does anything come to mind that feels true enough to actually stop you, even briefly?
